products.name: First Flush Whole Leaf
products.description: The first pluck of spring, whole leaf — bright, floral, and carrying the muscatel character Darjeeling first flush is famous for.
products.longDescription: The first flush is a race against the sun: leaves picked in the earliest weeks after winter dormancy, when the bush has stored a season's worth of aromatics. Grown above 3,500 ft in the Rungbong Valley, withered long and fired light, this tea brews pale gold rather than red. Each pack is whole leaf, light in the cup, and best drunk without milk so nothing stands between you and the spring.

brewingGuide.notes: Skip the milk — first flush is prized for its bright muscatel aromatics, and a slightly cooler pour keeps them intact.

products.name: First Flush Broken Leaf
products.description: Broken-leaf Darjeeling first flush — the same spring character with a quicker, stronger brew.
products.longDescription: Same garden, same pluck, smaller cut. Breaking the leaf exposes more surface to the water, so a broken-leaf first flush gives up its colour and briskness in half the time a whole leaf takes. You keep the muscatel note and trade a little of the floral top end for body — the everyday Darjeeling for people who find whole leaf too delicate for a morning cup.

brewingGuide.notes: Broken leaf brews faster and stronger than whole leaf — shorten the steep rather than the leaf.

products.name: First Flush Broken Mixed
products.description: A robust mixed broken grade from the Darjeeling spring harvest — strong, brisk, and happy to take milk.
products.longDescription: From the warmer, lower slopes below Kurseong, where the bush wakes earlier and grows faster. That makes a bolder, maltier cup with more colour and less of the ethereal floral note you get at altitude — which is exactly what you want in a tea that has to stand up to milk and sugar. The most versatile grade we sell, and the best value per cup.

brewingGuide.notes: A full boil and a longer steep bring out the malty depth — this grade takes milk happily.

products.name: First Flush Fannings
products.description: Fine Darjeeling first flush fannings — fast-brewing and full-strength. The working tea of the Darjeeling hills.
products.longDescription: Fannings are the finest cut: the smallest particles sifted from the same first flush pluck. More surface area means near-instant extraction, a deep coppery colour, and a cup with real backbone. This is not a contemplative tea and does not pretend to be — it is the grade the hills actually drink every morning, and it makes the best masala chai in the catalogue.

brewingGuide.notes: Fannings brew fast and strong — watch the clock, or lean in and make masala chai.

products.name: Second Flush
products.description: The summer pluck brings the deeper, fruitier side of Darjeeling. The lots are still with the garden — arriving after the summer harvest.

products.name: Third Flush
products.description: The third pluck of the year rounds things out with a mellow, coppery cup. Arriving after the autumn harvest.

products.name: First Flush
products.description: The first pluck of spring — a bright, floral Darjeeling with the light muscatel lift the season is known for.
products.longDescription: First flush leaves are picked in the first weeks after winter, when the bush is full of stored aromatics. The cup brews pale gold rather than red, light in body and fragrant, and is best drunk plain so nothing stands between you and the spring.

brewingGuide.notes: Skip the milk — a slightly cooler pour keeps the bright spring aromatics intact.

products.name: Golden Needle
products.description: Golden-tipped buds that brew a rounded, honeyed cup — the richest tea in the range.
products.longDescription: Golden Needle is made from tender buds that turn a deep gold as they are rolled and oxidised. The cup is smooth and full, with a natural sweetness that holds up to a second and third steep.

brewingGuide.notes: Rich enough to take a splash of milk, but try the first cup plain.

products.name: Green Tea
products.description: Unoxidised Darjeeling leaf — fresh, grassy and gentle, for an everyday lighter cup.
products.longDescription: Green tea is heated soon after plucking to stop oxidation, which keeps the leaf green and the cup fresh. Brew it cooler and shorter than black tea; boiling water draws out bitterness.

brewingGuide.notes: Let boiled water rest for a few minutes first — too hot and the cup turns bitter.

products.name: Pan Roasted
products.description: Leaf fired in a hot pan by hand, giving a toasty, nutty green tea with a soft finish.
products.longDescription: Instead of steaming, the leaf is tossed in a heated pan to stop oxidation. The fire adds a gentle toasted, nutty character on top of the fresh green notes.

brewingGuide.notes: A little hotter than other green teas brings out the roasted notes.

products.name: Silver Needle
products.description: Downy silver buds, simply withered and dried — the most delicate cup we make.
products.longDescription: Silver Needle uses only the unopened bud, covered in fine white hairs. It is barely processed, so the cup is pale, light and subtly sweet. Give it time: the buds open slowly.

brewingGuide.notes: The buds are bulky, so use more by volume and a longer steep than you would for black tea.

products.name: White Tea
products.description: Gently withered leaf and bud — soft, sweet and lightly floral.
products.longDescription: White tea is withered and dried with as little handling as possible. It brews a pale, mellow cup with a soft sweetness, and rewards several short steeps.

brewingGuide.notes: Keep the water below boiling and do not rush it.

gardens.name: Gopaldhara
story: Gopaldhara sits in the Rungbong Valley above Mirik, and its upper sections are among the highest planted land in Darjeeling — rising past 7,000 feet. Altitude is the whole story here: at that height the bush grows slowly, the internodes shorten, and the leaf concentrates the aromatics that give Darjeeling first flush its muscatel signature.

The first flush is a narrow window. After winter dormancy the bushes push a small quantity of tender two-leaves-and-a-bud, and the pluck runs for a few weeks in late February through April. That leaf is withered long and fired light, which is why a first flush brews pale gold rather than red, and why it should never meet milk.

Our whole leaf and broken leaf grades come from this valley. The same day's pluck is sorted into grades rather than blended across gardens, so a broken leaf here is not a lesser tea — it is the same leaf, cut for a faster, stronger cup.

gardens.name: Rohini
story: Rohini lies lower down the hill, on the slopes below Kurseong where the Darjeeling foothills warm earlier in the season. Lower elevation means the bushes wake sooner, so Rohini is often among the first gardens in the district to send out a first flush at all.

A warmer, faster-growing leaf makes a bolder cup — more body, more malt, less of the ethereal floral top note you get at 7,000 feet. That suits the broken mixed and fannings grades, which are built for strength: a fast brew, a full colour, and enough backbone to take milk or become masala chai.
Nothing here is blended with leaf from outside the district. The grade changes; the garden and the harvest do not.
